scenario.name: Microsoft, CISA & MITRE — Active Directory DCSync: Rogue MS-DRSR Replication & Security Event ID 4662 Forensics
scenario.shortSubtitle: Active Directory · DRSUAPI IDL_DRSGetNCChanges, Extended Rights GUIDs & EID 4662/4624 Correlation
scenario.overview: Imagine twin sovereign mint towers joined high above the city by an armored glass bridge built exclusively for peer mints to synchronize their master coin dies. When an old service ribbon accidentally left on the gatehouse grants full bridge courier privileges to an ordinary side-street van, the impostor rolls up beneath the archway, flashes the ribbon, and receives an exact duplicate of the mint’s crown seal without ever stepping foot inside the vault, until the bridge audit tower compares the side-street license plate against the official mint roster, locks down the bridge gate to verified towers only, and recasts the crown seals twice. In this scenario (T1003.006, Active Directory DCSync Rogue Replication & Event ID 4662 Forensics) between WKS-ADMIN-07 and CORP-DC01, an adversary abusing delegated domain replication permissions extracts krbtgt and account password hashes remotely along one continuous intrusion path without executing any tool on the Domain Controller. First, the attacker leverages over-privileged replication permissions on the domain root, then invokes MS-DRSR IDL_DRSGetNCChanges from a non-Domain-Controller workstation to stream secrets out of memory, then leaves an unmistakable Security Event ID 4662 and Event ID 4624 correlation trail, and finally faces Tier-0 ACL revocation and double krbtgt rotation. Steps #1 through #4 trace each Active Directory replication handoff and SIEM correlation step, while the Memory Forensics section compares legitimate peer Domain Controller replication against rogue non-DC DRSUAPI access.

stages.title: Over-Privileged Domain Root ACL (DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All)
stages.subtitle: Non-DC Service Account Retains Extended Rights GUID 1131f6ad-...
stages.description: Before a single ledger crosses the elevated glass bridge, the weakness already sits quietly inside the mint gatehouse registry. An outdated gold courier ribbon was accidentally left pinned to a regular side-street delivery account, quietly giving it the exact same bridge clearance reserved for sovereign mint towers. Active Directory controls which accounts may replicate password hashes via two extended rights stored on the domain root nTSecurityDescriptor (the security ACL on DC=corp,DC=local): DS-Replication-Get-Changes (GUID 1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2, permitting directory delta queries) and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All (GUID 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2, permitting replication of secret password hashes). Leaving both rights on a non-DC service account such as svc_dir_sync grants silent domain-wide credential replication. Organizations often grant replication rights temporarily during legacy directory sync deployments (such as Azure AD Connect staging or migration tools) and forget to revoke them afterward. Because Active Directory evaluates MS-DRSR replication strictly against the caller’s security token and the domain root DACL, not whether the caller is actually a Domain Controller computer account, any compromised non-DC account holding 1131f6aa and 1131f6ad effectively holds the keys to the kingdom. Auditing Security Event ID 5136 for nTSecurityDescriptor changes and running regular Tier-0 ACL reviews catch exposed replication ribbons before an adversary ever abuses them. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ REPLICATION ACL CHECK / ⇠#1 ACK 1131f6ad) from Node ① (#1 WKS-ADMIN-07 (10.20.14.88)) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM EID 4662 + Zeek).

stages.title: Rogue MS-DRSR IDL_DRSGetNCChanges Request From Non-DC Workstation
stages.subtitle: Impersonating a Peer Domain Controller Over DRSUAPI Without Touching Disk
stages.description: Rolling right up to the armored bridge ramp in an ordinary side-street service car, the impostor flashes the over-privileged ribbon and asks the north mint tower to stream down a fresh copy of the royal crown die ledger, without ever setting a single boot inside the north vault hallway. Using the MS-DRSR protocol (Microsoft Directory Replication Service Remote Protocol, exposed via DRSUAPI UUID e3514235-4b06-11d1-ab04-00c04fc2dcd2 over dynamic RPC TCP ports), the remote workstation invokes IDL_DRSGetNCChanges (Opnum 3, the legitimate peer-to-peer Active Directory replication call) directly against CORP-DC01. Because the Domain Controller fulfills the RPC call from lsass.exe memory, zero files are written and zero tools execute on the Domain Controller itself. Traditional endpoint monitoring focused solely on processes spawned on CORP-DC01 misses DCSync completely because the Domain Controller is simply performing its normal replication role inside lsass.exe via ntdsai.dll (the core Active Directory engine DLL that serves directory replication requests directly from memory). However, network sensors see the contradiction immediately: peer Active Directory replication over DRSUAPI Opnum 3 (the RPC procedure number dedicated to IDL_DRSGetNCChanges directory replication) should originate exclusively from known Domain Controller IP addresses (10.20.10.10, 10.20.10.11). When Zeek DCE-RPC or Suricata SID 2043901 observes 10.20.14.88 (WKS-ADMIN-07) invoking DRSGetNCChanges against CORP-DC01 targeting CN=krbtgt, defenders obtain indisputable wire-level proof of unauthorized replication. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ IDL_DRSGetNCChanges / ⇠#2 RESP Opnum 3) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 DC=corp,DC=local ACL), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM EID 4662 + Zeek).

stages.title: Security Event ID 4662 + Event ID 4624 SubjectLogonId Correlation
stages.subtitle: Catching Non-Machine DCSync Activity Despite Zero DC Endpoint Execution
stages.description: Even though the side-street van never crossed the vault threshold, the elevated bridge gatehouse automatically stamps an indelible blue ledger line recording every master-die transfer. Comparing that transfer badge against the city traffic log immediately exposes an ordinary street plate masquerading as a peer mint tower. When Directory Service Access auditing is configured properly on Domain Controllers, every DRSUAPI replication request writes Windows Security Event ID 4662 (An operation was performed on an object) with AccessMask 0x100 (Control Access) and Properties containing GUID 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2. Filtering out legitimate Domain Controller computer accounts (ending in $) and joining SubjectLogonId to Security Event ID 4624 reveals both the abused user (svc_dir_sync) and the exact rogue workstation IP (10.20.14.88). In a healthy domain, 99.9% of Security Event ID 4662 replication entries show SubjectUserName ending in $ (representing legitimate peer Domain Controller machine accounts such as CORP-DC02$) and originate from peer Domain Controller IPs. Here, CORP-DC01 records Event ID 4662 with SubjectUserName=svc_dir_sync, SubjectLogonId=0x39e4c2a (the unique session identifier linking this object-access audit record back to the caller’s network authentication event), ObjectType=domainDNS, and Properties containing {1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2}. Joining SubjectLogonId 0x39e4c2a to the matching Security Event ID 4624 network logon exposes IpAddress=10.20.14.88 (WKS-ADMIN-07) within milliseconds, giving SOC analysts complete host, identity, and timestamp attribution without needing a single EDR event on the DC. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ EID 4662 + 4624 JOIN / ⇠#3 ACK 0x100) from Node ③ (#3 DC=corp,DC=local ACL) to Node ④ (#4 CORP-DC01 (MS-DRSR)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM EID 4662 + Zeek).

keySpecs.value: No Binary Dropped & No NTDS.dit File Read on CORP-DC01

stages.title: Tier-0 ACL Revocation, Double krbtgt Rotation & Protected Users Hardening
stages.subtitle: Closing Unauthorized Replication Paths & Invalidating Forged TGT Risk
stages.description: With the rogue side-street car identified, mint security officers strip the misconfigured ribbon off the gatehouse ledger, quarantine the impostor van, lower an emerald peer-mint-only lock across the elevated bridge, and recast the master crown seals twice so any stolen stamp becomes worthless. Because DCSync exposes the krbtgt password hash (the master Kerberos signing secret that can mint forged Golden Tickets valid for years), remediation requires four disciplined actions: removing unauthorized replication ACEs from DC=corp,DC=local, isolating WKS-ADMIN-07, resetting krbtgt twice (separated by at least 10 hours to flush both current and previous Kerberos key versions), and enrolling Tier-0 admins into the Protected Users group. Simply resetting the compromised svc_dir_sync password is never sufficient after a confirmed DCSync event: an attacker who replicated CN=krbtgt retains silent domain persistence until krbtgt is rotated twice (allowing active Kerberos TGTs, default 10-hour lifetime, to cycle cleanly between resets so domain authentication stays uninterrupted). Simultaneously, defenders remove DS-Replication-Get-Changes and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All from every non-DC identity, audit AdminSDHolder, enforce Windows Firewall IPSec / DC-only allowlists on RPC replication ports, and keep continuous Event ID 4662 + Zeek DRSUAPI alerting permanently armed. On the diagram, follow Step #4 / Link #4 (#4→ TIER-0 ERADICATION / ⇠#4 ACK 2x Reset) from Node ④ (#4 CORP-DC01 (MS-DRSR)) to Node ⑤ (#5 NTDS Secret Store), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM EID 4662 + Zeek).

detectionRule.title: Non-DC Principal Granted Active Directory DCSync Extended Rights
detectionRule.ruleCode:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID in (5136, 4662)
| where Properties has_any ("1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2", "1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$" and SubjectUserName !in ("SYSTEM", "MSOL_")
detectionRule.mitigation: Audit DC=domain root ACLs regularly via BloodHound/PingCastle and revoke DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All from every non-Domain Controller principal.

detectionRule.title: Active Directory DCSync Detected via Security Event ID 4662
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: Active Directory DCSync Replication From Non-Machine Account
status: stable
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4662
    AccessMask: '0x100'
    Properties|contains:
      - '1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2'
      - '1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2'
  filter_dc:
    SubjectUserName|endswith: '$'
  condition: selection and not filter_dc
level: critical

steps.plainTitle: Rogue MS-DRSR IDL_DRSGetNCChanges Request From Non-DC Workstation
steps.storyAnalogy: Rolling right up to the armored bridge ramp in an ordinary side-street service car, the impostor flashes the over-privileged ribbon and asks the north mint tower to stream down a fresh copy of the royal crown die ledger, without ever setting a single boot inside the north vault hallway.
steps.simpleExplanation: Using the MS-DRSR protocol (Microsoft Directory Replication Service Remote Protocol, exposed via DRSUAPI UUID e3514235-4b06-11d1-ab04-00c04fc2dcd2 over dynamic RPC TCP ports), the remote workstation invokes IDL_DRSGetNCChanges (Opnum 3, the legitimate peer-to-peer Active Directory replication call) directly against CORP-DC01. Because the Domain Controller fulfills the RPC call from lsass.exe memory, zero files are written and zero tools execute on the Domain Controller itself.
steps.howItWorksInPractice: Traditional endpoint monitoring focused solely on processes spawned on CORP-DC01 misses DCSync completely because the Domain Controller is simply performing its normal replication role inside lsass.exe via ntdsai.dll (the core Active Directory engine DLL that serves directory replication requests directly from memory). However, network sensors see the contradiction immediately: peer Active Directory replication over DRSUAPI Opnum 3 (the RPC procedure number dedicated to IDL_DRSGetNCChanges directory replication) should originate exclusively from known Domain Controller IP addresses (10.20.10.10, 10.20.10.11). When Zeek DCE-RPC or Suricata SID 2043901 observes 10.20.14.88 (WKS-ADMIN-07) invoking DRSGetNCChanges against CORP-DC01 targeting CN=krbtgt, defenders obtain indisputable wire-level proof of unauthorized replication.
steps.diagramAlignment: Follow Step #2 / Link #2 as Node 1 (WKS-ADMIN-07) sends DRSUAPI Opnum 3 to Node 3 (CORP-DC01 MS-DRSR) to read Node 4 (NTDS Secret Store) while Node 5 (SIEM + Zeek) flags the non-DC source IP.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Deploy Suricata SID 2043901 and Zeek DCE-RPC sensors to fire P1 alerts whenever DRSUAPI UUID e3514235-4b06-11d1-ab04-00c04fc2dcd2 Opnum 3 (IDL_DRSGetNCChanges) originates from any IP address outside the authorized Domain Controller subnet.

steps.plainTitle: Security Event ID 4662 + Event ID 4624 SubjectLogonId Correlation
steps.storyAnalogy: Even though the side-street van never crossed the vault threshold, the elevated bridge gatehouse automatically stamps an indelible blue ledger line recording every master-die transfer. Comparing that transfer badge against the city traffic log immediately exposes an ordinary street plate masquerading as a peer mint tower.
steps.simpleExplanation: When Directory Service Access auditing is configured properly on Domain Controllers, every DRSUAPI replication request writes Windows Security Event ID 4662 (An operation was performed on an object) with AccessMask 0x100 (Control Access) and Properties containing GUID 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2. Filtering out legitimate Domain Controller computer accounts (ending in $) and joining SubjectLogonId to Security Event ID 4624 reveals both the abused user (svc_dir_sync) and the exact rogue workstation IP (10.20.14.88).
steps.howItWorksInPractice: In a healthy domain, 99.9% of Security Event ID 4662 replication entries show SubjectUserName ending in $ (representing legitimate peer Domain Controller machine accounts such as CORP-DC02$) and originate from peer Domain Controller IPs. Here, CORP-DC01 records Event ID 4662 with SubjectUserName=svc_dir_sync, SubjectLogonId=0x39e4c2a (the unique session identifier linking this object-access audit record back to the caller’s network authentication event), ObjectType=domainDNS, and Properties containing {1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2}. Joining SubjectLogonId 0x39e4c2a to the matching Security Event ID 4624 network logon exposes IpAddress=10.20.14.88 (WKS-ADMIN-07) within milliseconds, giving SOC analysts complete host, identity, and timestamp attribution without needing a single EDR event on the DC.
steps.diagramAlignment: Follow Step #3 / Link #3 as Node 3 (CORP-DC01) emits Security Event ID 4662 into Node 5 (SIEM EID 4662 + Zeek), which correlates SubjectLogonId 0x39e4c2a back to Node 1 (10.20.14.88).
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Run a real-time Sigma/KQL SIEM correlation rule matching Security Event ID 4662 (Properties containing GUID 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 with non-$ SubjectUserName) joined on SubjectLogonId to Security Event ID 4624 to pinpoint the rogue source IpAddress.

steps.plainTitle: Tier-0 ACL Revocation, Double krbtgt Rotation & Protected Users Hardening
steps.storyAnalogy: With the rogue side-street car identified, mint security officers strip the misconfigured ribbon off the gatehouse ledger, quarantine the impostor van, lower an emerald peer-mint-only lock across the elevated bridge, and recast the master crown seals twice so any stolen stamp becomes worthless.
steps.simpleExplanation: Because DCSync exposes the krbtgt password hash (the master Kerberos signing secret that can mint forged Golden Tickets valid for years), remediation requires four disciplined actions: removing unauthorized replication ACEs from DC=corp,DC=local, isolating WKS-ADMIN-07, resetting krbtgt twice (separated by at least 10 hours to flush both current and previous Kerberos key versions), and enrolling Tier-0 admins into the Protected Users group.
steps.howItWorksInPractice: Simply resetting the compromised svc_dir_sync password is never sufficient after a confirmed DCSync event: an attacker who replicated CN=krbtgt retains silent domain persistence until krbtgt is rotated twice (allowing active Kerberos TGTs, default 10-hour lifetime, to cycle cleanly between resets so domain authentication stays uninterrupted). Simultaneously, defenders remove DS-Replication-Get-Changes and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All from every non-DC identity, audit AdminSDHolder, enforce Windows Firewall IPSec / DC-only allowlists on RPC replication ports, and keep continuous Event ID 4662 + Zeek DRSUAPI alerting permanently armed.
steps.diagramAlignment: Follow Step #4 / Link #4 as Node 5 (SIEM EID 4662 + Zeek) cleans Node 2 (DC=corp,DC=local ACL) and locks down Node 3 (CORP-DC01 MS-DRSR) to peer Domain Controllers only.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Verify zero non-DC principals retain GUID 1131f6aa/1131f6ad on DC=corp,DC=local, confirm both krbtgt password resets appear in Security Event ID 4738 separated by >= 10 hours, and validate Tier-0 Protected Users membership.
